bearings.paper_claim: People do not select into SNS use at random, and selection differs by site and demographic group. Pew 2013 logistic coefficients (full sample, N 1,510 to 1,528, log-odds): female on Facebook 0.46 (p<.001), female on LinkedIn -0.39 (p<.01), Black on Twitter 0.63 (p<.01). Black on Facebook -0.31 is p<.10 only and -0.06 among Internet users, so it is not a reliable selection effect. Users of one platform are not the population.
bearings.paper_location: Table 1 (p. 68); sampling-frame section (pp. 64-65); Burke and Kraut discussion (pp. 65-66); conclusion (pp. 73-74)
bearings.system_side: social_interaction_layer.py: X reposts 1.0, X mentions 0.4, Bluesky mentions 0.4; pair p = events / max(25, X-post count of author), cap 0.25, so Bluesky events enter the numerator only (confirmed). build_multilayer_network.py: new edge w = 6p/(1-p) cap 2.0, or up to +30 percent reinforcement on existing ties (confirmed). Read-only counts from social_media.db on 2026-10-09: 411 Bluesky mentions = 392 D to D, 8 D to I, 5 I to D, 6 R to R, 0 D to R; 135 posters = 117 D, 16 R, 2 I; roster 533 = 259 D, 271 R, 3 I; posts 2023-07-01 to 2026-09-19. JSON written 2026-09-19 holds 739 pairs, 275 reposts, 953 mentions (X and Bluesky). Unverified: rows present at JSON write time, since the DB was modified 2026-10-04.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Her coefficients do not transfer; her frame logic may. Her data are US adults (2013) and one 2009-2012 student cohort, not legislators or Bluesky. That X adoption bias is mostly gone for legislators is the analyst's inference: the paper never discusses institutional accounts (502 of 515 member rows have an X handle, read-only). The Bluesky handle field is populated for all 515 rows, so 135 is posting, not account adoption. Party-skewed posting may carry a party-skewed edge pattern into the layer; untested, UNVERIFIED (DE-062).
bearings.verifier_note: Counts and code confirmed exactly. Softened: (1) none cross party holds only for D vs R; 13 mentions cross the D/I line. (2) Black on Facebook is p<.10 only. (3) The X-adoption claim is analyst inference, not the paper's. (4) Denominators 515 (db) and 533 (roster) must be named at each figure.

bearings.paper_claim: Non-users are excluded from a site-based sampling frame by design. If selection is related to outcomes, results from users may reach the opposite conclusion about the wider population. Sampling should not be tied to the substantive question. The paper does not discuss how missing social-media activity should be coded.
bearings.system_side: build_media_blend.py: SOCIAL_W = 0.5; f = min(1, nz/15), with nz the members carrying a nonzero social value in the category (shrink on by default). Cell = (1 - 0.5f) x press/p80 + 0.5f x social/p80. A member with no social value gets sv = 0, so at f = 1 the press side is halved and silence scores as zero, not missing (confirmed at lines 29, 463, 479). The downstream Press Release - Raw link was not checked.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper gives no evidence about missing-data coding. The concern bites only if posters differ from non-posters on stance in categories where f = 1; that is untested, and the analyst's own note says so. The stance-ladder rule on missing evidence was not checked. UNVERIFIED.
bearings.verifier_note: Code and formula confirmed. The paper supports the selection concern, not the zero-coding critique, so this is an analyst extension rather than a paper claim. Strength lowered from moderate to weak.

bearings.paper_claim: A sampling frame tied to the outcome can bias findings (Schwartz et al. 2013 opt-in app users, p. 65). Studies should state the frame scope and keep sampling separate from the outcome.
bearings.paper_location: pp. 65-66 (selection on the dependent variable); conclusion (pp. 73-74)
bearings.system_side: cu_text_collector.R lines 112-140: every CU-candidate-titled page is fetched; generic pages are capped at CAP = 1000 per member, newest first (confirmed). Registry figures (P(CU-relevant given CU title) 0.825 vs 0.0089; coverage D 92.5 vs R 87, Senate 83 vs House 96) match the component registry text; not re-measured from the corpus.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Hargittai's argument applies only if coverage gaps correlate with CU stance or volume. The cap drops only generic pages (about 0.9 percent CU-relevant per the registry). The cap is not party- or chamber-specific, so 'favours House and Democratic offices' does not follow from the code; it rests on unmeasured coverage rates. The collector comment assumes the skipped bulk is missing at random, which is the untested premise.
bearings.verifier_note: Code confirmed. The party and chamber skew is not supported by the cap itself. Limit the claim to: coverage depends on archive depth and title signal; party and chamber effect unmeasured here.

summary_issues: Overstated: 'age, education, income, gender and race each predict use of Facebook, LinkedIn and Twitter'. Gender is null for Twitter (-0.00), income is null for Facebook among Internet users (-0.12), and Hispanic is null for all three. Should say each predicts use of at least one site.
The 0.72 (LinkedIn, logged income) and -1.37 (LinkedIn, high school or less) are log-odds coefficients from the full Pew sample (N 1,510 for LinkedIn), not effect sizes. Name the scale and window.
'A biased sampling frame can reverse the direction of a finding' overstates the paper's 'may come to the exact opposite conclusion' (p. 74). Use 'may'.
'Legislators are elite accounts, so platform adoption bias mostly disappears on X' is the analyst's inference, not the paper's; the paper never discusses institutional accounts. Mark it as inference.
'none cross party' holds only for D vs R. The same paragraph's counts show 8 D to I and 5 I to D mentions; state that 13 cross the D/I line.

Denominators are mixed: 502 of 515 have an X handle (social_media.db members table, 515 rows) while party counts use the 533 roster. The Bluesky handle field is populated for all 515 rows, so 135 posters is posting, not account adoption. Name the denominator at each figure.

The UIC panel 2012 figures (Facebook 89, Twitter 38, LinkedIn 18 percent) come from a 2012 wave with 52 percent return and no N in Table 3; name that. 'UIC students' should read young adults in one required first-year class (2009 wave n = 547).
Paul-alignment claims (Fink framework; critiques on sign, third-party sentiment and temporal weighting) were not checked against his annotation files; treat as unverified.

Extraction issues in ext: the 'space constraints' limitation is on p. 66, not p. 65; Black on Facebook -0.31 and Asian on LinkedIn -0.29 need p<.10 flags; 'no single SNS can serve as a sampling frame' is the extractor's inference, while the paper says the usage rates should give pause (p. 71).

Coverage: all 3 bearings and all 4 related links checked; Tables 1, 3 and 4 re-read in the paper text; code ranges re-read; DB and roster counts re-derived read-only.
